source: Inoue et al. (2025) Wider or Deeper? Scaling LLM Inference-Time Compute with Adaptive Branching Tree Search (AB-MCTS)
finding: Closest published test of gap 1. Thompson sampling decides at each node whether to widen (new child) or deepen (refine a child). No fixed branching factor. Compared with repeated sampling, sequential refinement and standard UCT-MCTS at the same number of generation calls. AB-MCTS gets the best average rank on MLE-Bench and is above or level with the baselines on LiveCodeBench, CodeContest and ARC-AGI.
numbers: Budget is generation calls (2^7 = 128 max; ARC-AGI up to 512 with DeepSeek-V3), not tokens. MLE-Bench (GPT-4o, 3 competitions) average rank: AB-MCTS-M 1.3, sequential refinement 2.3, repeated sampling 3.0, standard MCTS 3.3. ARC-AGI GPT-4o Pass@2: repeated sampling 15.0, AB-MCTS-A (Beta) 14.0, AB-MCTS-A (Gaussian) 13.0, AB-MCTS-M 12.3, standard MCTS 9.0, sequential refinement 8.7. With DeepSeek-V3 at 200 to 500 calls AB-MCTS keeps improving while repeated sampling plateaus.
quote: The UCT score is inapplicable to our AB-MCTS because GEN nodes make the problem fundamentally different from a standard multi-armed bandit problem
limits: The bandit is over widen vs deepen, not over problem classes. Calls, not tokens. On ARC-AGI repeated sampling is the best baseline at GPT-4o scale and AB-MCTS only matches it. The authors say GEN nodes have no children, so UCT cannot score them, which is why they use Thompson sampling.
agent_relevance: Supports Thompson-style widen/deepen choice as a tested pattern in an LLM tree. Does not answer the per-class pass-rate question. An equal-token test is still not published.

source: Inoue et al. (2025) AB-MCTS, Appendix C.4: comparison with progressive widening (fixed-rule widening)
finding: A fixed progressive-widening rule (children bounded by k times visits^alpha) can match the adaptive Thompson rule, but only at the right (k, alpha). Nearest published fixed-width vs adaptive-width test at equal calls.
numbers: LiveCodeBench Pass@1, deepseek-v3-0324, budget 2^7, n=5: PW (1, 0.45) 48.7 +-0.8; PW (5, 0.5) 50.7 +-1.3; PW (10, 0.55) 50.5 +-3.1; AB-MCTS-A Gaussian 48.9 +-2.0; AB-MCTS-A Beta 51.8 +-1.4; AB-MCTS-M 49.6 +-1.6.
limits: All differences are within about one to two standard deviations. Best PW setting is level with AB-MCTS. Authors report PW is sensitive to its parameters, and (10, 0.55) had the highest variance. One benchmark, one model.
agent_relevance: Honest reading: adaptive widening buys robustness to tuning, not a large mean gain. Judge a per-class widen rule by variance across classes, not only mean pass rate.

source: Zuo and Zhu (2026, v2) Strategic Scaling of Test-Time Compute: A Bandit Learning Approach
finding: Test-time compute allocation across queries is framed as pure-exploration bandit learning. Under the same compute budget as uniform allocation, the adaptive algorithms put more samples on hard-but-solvable queries and spend less on unsolvable ones.
numbers: Gains over uniform allocation at the same budget: up to +11.10 points (15.04% relative) on MATH-500, +10.82 (14.44% relative) on AIME25, +11.23 (15.29% relative) on LiveCodeBench. The framework handles streaming and token-constrained settings.
limits: The bandit is over queries (items), not over idea classes inside one tree. Figures are best-case ('up to'); I read the abstract and introduction, not every table.
agent_relevance: Strongest equal-compute evidence that a bandit allocator beats uniform allocation for LLM sampling. Their unit is the question; ours would be the class. Same logic, untested at our level.

source: Harris and Slivkins (2026, v4) Should You Use Your Large Language Model to Explore or Exploit? (UAI 2026)
finding: Frontier reasoning models (GPT-5 family) fix the exploit half on raw history: GPT-5-mini is perfect on a 5-arm bandit task of naming the best empirical arm, for every gap and history length, where GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 degrade with longer history and smaller gap. On contextual bandits GPT-5 beats GPT-4 of similar size, but all LLMs stay below plain linear regression, and GPT-4 with a code interpreter beats GPT-5.2. LLMs do help as exploration oracles that propose candidate actions in large semantic action spaces.
numbers: MAB exploit puzzle: 5 arms, means 1/2 +- gap/2, 10 tasks per gap, gaps 0 to 0.5. GPT-5-mini FracCorrect = 1 for all gaps and T. Models: GPT-5.2, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-3, Mistral-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. GPT-5.2 priced at $1.25 per 1M input and $10 per 1M output tokens, about 60 tokens/s.
quote: LLMs ... consistently underperform relative to a simple linear regression, even in inherently non-linear tasks
limits: This tests exploiting a given history, not end-to-end exploration. Reasoning models were too slow or costly for large-scale runs and GPT-5 was not configured for tool use. Temperature did not matter. The authors cite Krishnamurthy 2024 and Nie 2024 for the end-to-end failure.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 2: reasoning models remove the arithmetic part of the failure (reading means from a log), but a code-computed table still beats free reasoning on harder tasks. Keep the code-computed per-class table.

source: Pan, Xie and Wilson (2025) Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively
finding: In Little Alchemy 2 (open-ended text task: combine elements to discover new ones, 500 trials) only reasoning models match or beat humans. Non-reasoning LLMs lean on uncertainty (try the least tried) and ignore empowerment (what the new element makes possible). Sparse-autoencoder analysis finds uncertainty and choice represented in early blocks and empowerment in later blocks, so fast models decide before empowerment is computed.
numbers: Elements discovered in 500 trials: Llama-3.1-8B 9; Llama-3.1-70B 25; GPT-4o 35; humans 42 (51 over all trials; 29,493 players); DeepSeek-R1 85; o1 177. Versus humans: o1 t=9.71 p<0.001; R1 t=3.40 p<0.027; GPT-4o t=-5.48 p<0.001. R1 used all seven reasoning labels and far more tokens per trial than GPT-4o.
quote: traditional LLMs ... think too fast and make premature decisions, hindering effective exploration
limits: One game, one model per family, temperatures 0 to 1 (o1 fixed at 1). Not a repeated-arm bandit. SAE analysis is on open models only, and the link between depth of thought and exploration is correlational.
agent_relevance: Direct answer to the second half of gap 2: extended thinking appears to close much of the exploration gap in an open-ended text task. Our tree is open-ended in the same way. A thinking-mode arm is worth testing against the code-table arm.

source: Anonymous authors (2026, v2) Exploration and Exploitation Errors Are Measurable for Language Model Agents
finding: 35 frontier LM agents in partially observable grid maps with a hidden task DAG. A policy-agnostic metric splits each unproductive step into exploration error or exploitation error. Log of both errors predicts success. A compact memory harness with no reasoning beat a reasoning baseline that keeps its own traces.
numbers: Success vs log error R2 = 0.885 (exploration) and 0.875 (exploitation); best models reach up to 100% success while many frontier models fail within the step budget. Table 3 as extracted (layout garbled): Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite reasoning 50.0% vs harness 76.9%; GPT-4.1 reasoning 66.7% vs harness 72.2%.
quote: Harness engineering without reasoning outperforms reasoning by utilizing historical outcomes.
limits: Table text came out of the PDF in misaligned columns, so the pairing of rows is my best reading. Synthetic maps; the Minecraft Clone extension is brief. Model names are as printed in the paper.
agent_relevance: Fresh 2026 support for K03: a code-built memory summary of what was tried beats free reasoning over a log, at lower budget. Also gives a way to count exploration errors apart from exploitation errors in our tree.

source: Semantic Bandits authors (2026) Semantic Bandits: In-Context Exploration-Exploitation is Biased by Semantic Priors (COLM 2026)
finding: Arms with meaningful text labels cut exploration. When labels agree with reward this helps; when they mislead it badly hurts. Negative rewards trigger more exploration than equal positive rewards. A summary (mean reward and pulls per arm) beat full raw history for Qwen3-32B. A sample trace suggests priors shrink but remain in a large reasoning model (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite with thinking).
numbers: Models: OLMo-3.1-32B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite (thinking tokens capped at 150 for OLMo and Qwen, unlimited for Gemini). OLMo barely explored unless told it was a bandit; Qwen3 explored with alphanumeric labels but pure-exploited with ordinal labels; Gemini explored quickly on most tasks except a clothing task with world-knowledge labels. Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B did not explore enough and were dropped.
limits: 3 to 5 arms and short horizons (turn 9 comparisons). Few frontier models. Regret tables sit in the appendix; I did not extract one headline number.
agent_relevance: Warning for our tree: if class names are descriptive, the model's prior about them biases widening. Use neutral class ids in the prompt, or make the widen choice in code.

source: Wellocate authors (2026) Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
finding: Five LLMs choose each round between trying a new candidate and re-testing a noisy reading. Three over-confirm (75 to 94 percent of slots re-testing); one under-confirms (14 percent); on the generated landscape every model's final pick is worse than a scripted rule. A list of untried candidates cuts re-testing; a ledger summary or landscape note changes it by at most 5 points.
numbers: Scripted rules re-test about 24% (guessing) and 38% (model-guided) of slots. Opus 4.7, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek V3.1: 75 to 94%. Gemini 3.1 Pro: 14%. GPT-6.1 Sol: 44%. On GB1 and PhoQ the best scripted rule re-tests at most 1%, yet every model re-tests more. A replayed final re-test round recovers only about a quarter of the loss.
limits: Simulated assay campaigns, not text ideas. Model names are as printed. The noisy check matches our 'reproducibility of the check' signal.
agent_relevance: Evidence for gap 4: LLM agents handle the re-check versus new-try split badly, and a menu of untried options helps more than a summary. Put the re-check rate in code, not in the model's judgement.

source: Chen et al. (2025) When Greedy Wins: Emergent Exploitation Bias in Meta-Bandit LLM Training
finding: SFT on expert trajectories and RL with regret-shaped or algorithmic rewards give LLM bandit agents with regret near UCB and Thompson sampling, but the gains come from greedier exploitation: more early catastrophic failure (abandoning exploration too soon) than the pretrained model. Agents trained to imitate UCB become more exploitative than the teacher and beat it on average.
numbers: RL-trained agents match SFT in distribution and generalise better out of distribution (abstract and introduction; no single headline number extracted).
limits: Training, not prompting, so not a scaffold test. I read the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Average regret hides lock-in. For our agent, track the share of runs where the solving branch is never revisited, not just mean pass rate.

source: Grams et al. (2025) Disentangling Exploration of Large Language Models by Optimal Exploitation
finding: Exploration is isolated as its own objective in a partly hidden state space. Missing reward is split into an exploration part and an exploitation part using the optimal achievable return. Most LLMs struggle to explore, and weak exploration is not enough. Exploration quality correlates positively with reasoning ability.
numbers: Abstract-level claim: positive correlation between exploration performance and reasoning capabilities. No single number extracted.
limits: Abstract and introduction only. Small tasks with hidden state.
agent_relevance: Second independent line saying reasoning ability helps exploration (see d05). Supports a thinking-mode comparison arm.

source: Gurjar et al. (2026, v2) DORA Explorer: Improving the Exploration Ability of LLMs Without Training
finding: Sampling several candidate actions and choosing by sequence-level log-probability rank (not temperature) raises exploration without training. Tested on a Bernoulli bandit (Llama-3.1 8B, T=500, 20 LLM runs vs 1000 for classical rules, with suffix failure reported) and on TALES text games.
numbers: TextWorld success for Qwen-2.5 7B: ReAct 31.43% to DORA 45.5%. Unique states visited in TextWorld, ScienceWorld and AlfWorld (Llama-3.1 8B) are higher than for zero-shot, CoT, ToT and ReAct.
limits: Small open models only. Gains are in action diversity, which can be noise rather than directed exploration.
agent_relevance: A training-free diversity knob for the widen step. Cheap to try, though it draws extra candidates per step.

source: Raileanu and Rocktaschel (2020) RIDE: Rewarding Impact-Driven Exploration for Procedurally-Generated Environments
finding: Independent comparison of RND, ICM and count bonuses on procedurally generated MiniGrid. In fixed mazes they work; in procedurally generated mazes they stall in early rooms. ICM drops under a noisy-TV ball. Their ICM reproduces the original ICM result on VizDoom and on Mario without extrinsic reward, but with extrinsic reward ICM hurts learning on Mario.
numbers: Procedurally generated MultiRoomN10S6: Count, RND and ICM reach the 4th, 3rd and 2nd room within an episode; RIDE explores all rooms. Mario with intrinsic plus extrinsic reward: ICM converges later and lower than IMPALA. VizDoom: RIDE equals ICM and all other baselines fail. Best coefficient 0.1 for ICM and RND, 0.005 for count. Added MiniGridN7S4NoisyTV: ICM performance drops.
limits: Written by authors of a competing method, so baseline tuning may favour RIDE. Curves are in plots; I extracted the text claims only.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 9: outside Atari, RND and ICM-style bonuses fail in procedurally generated tasks because 'novel' keeps resetting. Our trees are new every item, so use within-item (episodic) counts only.

source: Henaff, Raileanu, Jiang and Rocktaschel (2022) Exploration via Elliptical Episodic Bonuses (E3B)
finding: Benchmark of IMPALA, RND, RIDE, ICM and NovelD on 16 MiniHack sparse-reward tasks plus other suites. E3B (episodic elliptical bonus on inverse-dynamics features) beats all by a significant margin on median, IQM and mean. ICM and RIDE solve the singleton VizDoom sparse task, and the authors note ICM was designed for singleton MDPs. In reward-free Habitat exploration E3B reveals significantly more of unseen maps than ICM, RND and NovelD.
numbers: MiniHack: 16 tasks, 8 built on MiniGrid, bootstrapped CIs with the rliable protocol. Habitat: HM3D 1000 spaces, 3 seeds for error bars.
limits: Authors of a new method again. Gains are aggregate and in figures.
agent_relevance: Second source for K07/K09 outside Atari: cross-episode novelty bonuses degrade when the world changes each episode; per-episode bonuses recover it. Maps onto per-item pass-rate counts in our tree.

source: Burda, Edwards, Pathak et al. (2018) Large-Scale Study of Curiosity-Driven Learning
finding: Noisy-TV test with pixel and inverse-dynamics-feature curiosity in a Unity maze: adding a TV that changes channel on an action drastically slows learning. If run long enough the agents sometimes still converge to extrinsic reward.
numbers: Qualitative: drastic slowdown. No headline number in the text.
limits: Learned features only partly help; the authors call the stochasticity problem open.
agent_relevance: Anchor for gap 4: any widen signal that rewards surprise will pay for paraphrase noise.

source: Matiisen, Oliver, Cohen and Schulman (2017) Teacher-Student Curriculum Learning
finding: A bandit over tasks that rewards the slope of recent scores (learning progress), using absolute slope to catch forgetting. Four variants: Online (non-stationary bandit), Naive (practise K times, regress), Window (FIFO buffer of last K scores with linear regression) and Sampling (Thompson-style: sample one recent reward from each task's last-K buffer and take the highest). Sampling has no exploration hyperparameter.
numbers: 9-digit 1D addition: all variants beat uniform sampling and the best manual curriculum; Window best in 1D, Naive best in 2D, Sampling competitive in both. 2D addition: manual curriculum hard to beat and uniform sampling surprisingly efficient. Minecraft maze: unsolvable by direct training, solved by TSCL, about an order of magnitude faster than uniform sampling.
limits: No universal best variant; results come from plots. Learning progress needs several scores per task, so it is slow with few passes.
agent_relevance: Direct template for gap 5: a buffer of the last K pass/fail results per class, sampled Thompson-style, is a known no-tuning rule for drifting classes. Set K from our own history.

source: Graves, Bellemare, Menick, Munos and Kavukcuoglu (2017) Automated Curriculum Learning for Neural Networks
finding: Exp3.S adversarial bandit picks the next task; the reward is a learning-progress signal (prediction gain, gradient prediction gain, self prediction gain, target prediction gain). The paper notes prediction gain is a biased estimate of learning progress, and reduces noise in the gain by drawing a whole batch from one task.
numbers: Numerical results not extracted (I read the method sections).
limits: Method text only. The signals cost an extra forward or backward pass.
agent_relevance: Learning progress as the reward of a widen bandit is old and tested; its main noise control is to batch several samples per task before computing a gain. Matches the 'reproducibility of the check' option.

source: Garivier and Moulines (2008/2011) On Upper-Confidence Bound Policies for Non-Stationary Bandit Problems
finding: For rewards that change at unknown breakpoints, discounted UCB and sliding-window UCB are near rate optimal. Any policy with logarithmic regret in the stationary case has regret of order at least T / log T once breakpoints exist, so plain UCB1 cannot be trusted when class rates drift.
numbers: Regret O(sqrt(Y_T * T) * log T) for Y_T breakpoints. Window tau = 2B * sqrt(T log T / Y_T). In simulation D-UCB does about as well as SW-UCB and both detect breakpoints faster than UCB1 and EXP3.S; UCB1 takes very long to switch back after the second breakpoint (t=5000).
limits: Theory for abrupt change; two small Monte-Carlo examples with parameters tuned for the horizon. Needs Y_T known or guessed.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule for window length: it grows with the square root of the horizon. With a handful of tries per class the window is capped by the data, so a simple discount is easier.

source: Raj and Kalyani (2017) Taming Non-stationary Bandits: A Bayesian Approach (discounted Thompson sampling)
finding: Plain Thompson sampling has high regret in slowly and quickly varying environments. Discounting the Beta prior parameters (dTS) and an optimistic variant (dOTS) do well against SW-UCB, Discounted-UCB, REXP3, Dynamic TS and EXP3-IX in most settings. In abruptly changing settings the margin shrinks as arms grow.
numbers: Settings compared with SW-UCB: horizon 500 (fast varying) window 24, dTS gamma 0.40; horizon 2500 (slow) window 89, gamma 0.75; horizon 1000 (abrupt) window 37, gamma 0.60. Figure 2: with more arms dTS/dOTS keep a regret margin in slow and fast change but converge to the others under abrupt change.
limits: Bernoulli simulation with tuned parameters; margins are in plots. No LLM data.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 5 in principle: use discounted Thompson (decay the prior counts, gamma about 0.4 to 0.75) and tune the discount on our own pass-rate logs. TS beats UCB under slow or fast change, not under abrupt change.

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley and Clune (2023/2024) OMNI: Open-endedness via Models of human Notions of Interestingness (re-opened)
finding: Re-opened. Learning progress alone is distracted by boring learnable tasks, a noisy-TV-like failure in task space. Adding a foundation-model judgement of interestingness fixes much of it and comes close to a hand-built oracle.
numbers: Crafter: learning progress learns 55 tasks (9 interesting); OMNI 82 tasks (14 interesting). Mean success on interesting tasks 0.52 (LP) vs 0.78 (OMNI). OMNI vs LP significant, all p<1e-3 (Mann-Whitney). OMNI almost the same as the oracle (all but one p>0.05). New-task generation variant: LP learns 2 tasks, OMNI 13 (CI 11 to 17). The judge was GPT-3 Davinci for Crafter and GPT-4 for the generation setting.
limits: Same group's own benchmark. The judge was GPT-3 or GPT-4 only, so no replication across base models is shown. Interestingness examples are few-shot and hand-written.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (OMNI half): not replicated with other base models in this paper. Good analogue for paraphrase noise: learning progress is lured by variations of the same thing, and an LLM judge of 'is this really a new idea' removes them.

source: Monea, Bosselut, Brantley and Artzi (2025) LLMs Are In-Context Bandit Reinforcement Learners (COLM 2025, v4, re-opened)
finding: Re-opened. Tested across Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen2.5 from 0.5B to 72B, Gemini 1.5 Flash 8B and early Phi-3.5-mini. Naive in-context RL learns well only when negative-reward episodes are removed; Stochastic ICRL (random subsampling of past episodes) learns even with negatives and tolerates 10% flipped rewards. A reward signal is needed: none or inverted reward gives negligible gain.
numbers: Banking77: Qwen2.5-7B zero-shot 6.2% to 72.2% with Stochastic ICRL, no gold labels. Performance rises with model size across all Qwen sizes, and the method ordering holds across sizes. The appendix reward-ablation table came out misaligned in extraction, so I do not quote its cells.
limits: Many-label classification bandits, not tree search. 'Only positive is best' is stated in the Figure 3 caption; the table cells are scrambled in my extraction.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 (Monea half): the positive-only finding holds across Llama, Qwen sizes and Gemini Flash within this one paper. It maps to keeping only successful attempts in memory. But failures carry information, and subsampling episodes is the fix that keeps them.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: Archive-and-return with an LLM choosing which archived state to resume, which action to try and which states to keep. In text puzzles it beats Reflexion, ReAct, DFS and BFS. Ablating any of the three LLM steps lowers success, and classic visitation-frequency Go-Explore is far worse on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24 at 150 environment steps, 100 seeds: IGE 100%; classic visitation-frequency Go-Explore 38 +-22; ablations 61 to 96% (column labels partly scrambled in extraction). IGE reaches 100% on Game of 24 on average 70.8% faster than the next best baseline (DFS), chi-square p<0.05 at 150 operations. TextWorld Cooking Game: IGE beats ReAct by 36 points; Coin Collector: IGE the only method that solves it. With Claude 3.5 Sonnet on Game of 24, naive action selection 24% vs IGE 86%. All final experiments cost under 2,000 USD in API fees.
limits: Returning needs a simulator reset or a goal-conditioned policy, and the environments are deterministic. The cost axis is environment steps or operations, not tokens. Reflexion was omitted in one environment for cost.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 only partly closed: in Game of 24, where most failures are wrong partial ideas, archiving partial states and resuming helps a lot. In our tree a return is free (node text is stored), so the extra cost is the LLM call that picks the node. An equal-token test is not published.

source: Lange et al. (2025) ShinkaEvolve: Towards Open-Ended and Sample-Efficient Program Evolution
finding: Evolutionary code search uses (a) UCB1 over which LLM writes the next mutation, rewarded by exp of the relative gain over the parent, and (b) novelty rejection sampling: embed the mutable code with text-embedding-3-small and reject a proposal if cosine similarity to an archive member is above 0.95, then optionally ask an LLM judge. On circle packing, bandit LLM selection gives a slight gain over a fixed ensemble in the figure caption while the text calls it significant; embedding rejection clearly beats no rejection; the LLM novelty judge adds only a marginal gain.
numbers: Threshold 0.95 cosine, up to 3 novelty attempts, UCB1 exploration coefficient 1.0. Ablation results are in a figure (scores about 2.0 to 2.7 on circle packing), not in a table.
limits: Ablations on a single task. Caption and text disagree on the size of the bandit gain. Code embeddings, not natural-language ideas.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a code-embedding cosine of 0.95 works as a near-duplicate filter, and an LLM judge on top is not needed. It is a filter, not a bonus; nobody here uses it as a count.

source: Tam et al. (2022) Semantic Exploration from Language Abstractions and Pretrained Representations
finding: Novelty (RND and NGU-style kNN bonuses) computed in pretrained vision-language or text embedding space instead of raw pixels. Text embeddings of an oracle caption work best; image embeddings learned with language supervision come close; ImageNet embeddings sometimes hurt.
numbers: Playroom sample efficiency up 18 to 70%; about 50 to 70% on lift and put and 18 to 38% on find (image-based LSE); lift learned 33% faster; City coverage doubles; Lang-NGU on oracle text embeddings covers up to 3x the area of a pixel baseline. ImageNet embeddings hurt on the find task.
limits: 3D Unity environments with vision, not text ideas. The bonus is applied during training of the agent only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: an embedding pseudo-count can drive a bonus when the embedding is shaped by language, and the choice of embedding can flip the sign of the effect. Test our embedding for paraphrase invariance before using it as a count.

source: Kuhn, Gal and Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation (ICLR 2023)
finding: Counting distinct strings goes wrong because different strings can mean the same thing. They cluster samples by bidirectional entailment with DeBERTa-large and compute entropy over meaning clusters. This beats entropy over raw sequences and a lexical-similarity baseline for predicting whether an answer is correct.
numbers: Mean distinct meaning clusters per question: CoQA correct 1.27 vs incorrect 1.77; TriviaQA correct 1.89 vs incorrect 3.89. AUROC: CoQA semantic entropy 0.77 vs distinct-answer count 0.66; TriviaQA 0.83 vs 0.79.
limits: Short answers (TriviaQA, CoQA). Clustering cost grows with the square of the samples. Entailment on long multi-step ideas is untested here.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4: the standard paraphrase-safe way to count visits is to cluster by mutual entailment, not by embedding distance. A usable visit count for ideas is the number of meaning clusters.

source: Shaib et al. (2024, v3 2026) Standardizing the Measurement of Text Diversity: A Tool and a Comparative Analysis of Scores
finding: Compares many text diversity scores. Compression ratio is fast and tracks slow n-gram overlap scores. Compression ratio, long n-gram self-repetition and Self-BLEU have low mutual correlation, so reporting those three is enough. BERTScore-style embedding similarity was found limited. Text length confounds every score.
numbers: Qualitative; correlation matrices are in figures for CNN/DM and XSUM. No paraphrase-invariance test.
limits: Measures diversity of corpora, not whether two candidate ideas are the same. Does not test robustness to paraphrase directly.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: I found no study that checks which of these measures is stable when two texts differ only by paraphrase. Hold length fixed when using any of them as a bonus.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS), exploration-weight ablation, re-read
finding: The only exploration-weight test in LATS is on HotPotQA. Default w=1 gives EM 0.63 (LATS ReAct). w=0.5 gives 0.55. w=2.0 gives 0.63, the same as default, so a larger weight did not help; the authors say it gave faster convergence. They state the optimal setting depends on the environment and state-space complexity. No weight sweep on HumanEval, MBPP or WebShop.
numbers: HotPotQA, random subset of 100 questions, max depth 7: w=0.5 EM 0.55; default w=1 EM 0.63; w=2.0 EM 0.63. One point on 100 questions is 0.01, so the 0.08 drop at w=0.5 is 8 questions, from one run as far as the text says. The table row labels for the other ablations came out misaligned in extraction, so they are not quoted.
quote: The optimal setting depends on the particular environment and complexity of the state space.
limits: n=100 and no repeats or CIs reported. This corrects the earlier reading 'w=2.0 beats w=0.5' to 'w=2.0 equals default and w=0.5 is worse'. A class-dependent best weight is therefore untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Treat the weight as a hyperparameter to tune per task family on our own logs, and do not read the LATS table as showing that more exploration helps.
